The Roundtail chub Gila robusta is a cyprinid native to the Colorado River basin, attaining a maximum recorded total length of 43 centimeters [Li = 43 centimeters] in desert river habitats. Field surveys in the upper Verde River indicate that individuals typically reach a total length of 10.7 centimeters [Lp = 10.7 centimeters] at the onset of sexual maturity, a size that corresponds with the development of secondary sexual characteristics in males and the onset of vitellogenesis in females. Comparative data from congeneric species suggest this length threshold reflects a minimum energetic prerequisite for successful gonad maturation within the variable flow regimes characteristic of this species' native range. Populations occupying intermittent streams often show slightly delayed maturation relative to those in perennial reaches, presumably due to differences in food availability and thermal conditions.

Studies conducted under controlled laboratory conditions at 13 °C [T = 13 °C] have provided valuable insight into the reproductive potential of this species. At this stable thermal regime, mature females release approximately 274 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 274 eggs per spawning event] and can spawn daily during peak reproductive activity [F_R_i = spawn daily during peak reproductive activity], yielding a daily reproductive output of about 274 eggs per day [Ri = about 274 eggs per day]. This output is modulated by photoperiod and food ration, with peak fecundity occurring in early summer when prey resources are most abundant. The relatively cool temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C] corresponds to the typical spring spawning temperatures in the lower Colorado River tributaries, suggesting that the ultimate reproductive rate is closely tied to the thermal conditions experienced by natural populations.

The wet weight at birth for newly hatched yolk-sac larvae, based on an egg diameter comparable to that of the closely related Siphateles bicolor, is approximately 1.2 milligrams [Wwb = approximately 1.2 milligrams]. These tiny prolarvae, measuring only a few millimeters at eclosion, possess a large yolk reserve that sustains them during the first days of development prior to the onset of exogenous feeding. The larvae remain lecithotrophic for roughly five to seven days at 13 °C [T = 13 °C], after which they commence first exogenous feeding as the yolk-sac is fully resorbed. Successful recruitment depends critically on the temporal match between larval emergence and peaks in zooplankton abundance, a relationship that is tightly coupled to the thermal regime of the spawning habitat.

As adults, Roundtail chub can achieve an asymptotic wet weight estimated at 1054 grams [Wwi = 1054 grams], a body mass that is attained only by individuals in the most productive habitats. This value, derived from length-weight regressions applied to the ultimate total length, is consistent with the largest specimens sampled during a 2012 survey of the San Juan River. The relationship between body mass and fecundity is strongly positive, with the largest gravid females carrying substantially more oocytes than smaller conspecifics. Body condition indices in this species decline during the spawning season as energy reserves are mobilized for gamete production, and post-spawning mortality can be significant in years when prey resources are scarce.

The maximum lifespan of Gila robusta under natural conditions is approximately 8 years [am = approximately 8 years] in populations inhabiting the lower Colorado River basin at water temperatures averaging 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This longevity is intermediate among southwestern cyprinids, falling below the 15-year lifespan reported for the Colorado pikeminnow Ptychocheilus lucius but exceeding the 4-year maximum of the speckled dace Rhinichthys osculus. Age determination from otolith annuli suggests that most mortality occurs after the second or third spawning season, with senescent individuals showing reduced growth increments and diminished gonadal investment. The relatively cool thermal regime of 13 °C [T = 13 °C] appears to slow the rate of physiological aging, contributing to the extended reproductive window observed in this species.
